Make UC a Good Neighbor v. Regents of University of California

2024-06-06 · California Supreme Court · Official opinion

Question: Did a new state law defeat objections that UC Berkeley’s environmental report failed to study student social noise and alternative locations for its People’s Park housing project? [e1]

Background: UC Berkeley approved a long-range development plan and a housing project at People’s Park. The project proposed student beds, public open space, and affordable and supportive housing. An environmental impact report examined both the broad development plan and specific projects. Two groups challenged the report under the California Environmental Quality Act, or CEQA, arguing that it did not adequately analyze noise from student parties and pedestrians or alternatives to the People’s Park location. The trial court rejected their challenge, but the Court of Appeal agreed with those objections. While Supreme Court review was pending, the Legislature enacted Assembly Bill 1307 as an immediately effective law. It excluded specified residential occupant and guest noise from CEQA’s significant environmental effects and excused qualifying university housing projects from studying alternative locations. [e2]

Decision: The Supreme Court unanimously overturned the Court of Appeal’s judgment. It directed that the case return to the trial court for a judgment on the merits for the university respondents. The new law defeated the social-noise objections to both the People’s Park project and the residential portions of the development plan. The opponents conceded the project met the new law’s conditions for dispensing with alternative-site analysis. This lawsuit therefore presented no obstacle to the People’s Park project. [e1] [e3]

Justices on the Ballot

Joshua P. Groban: Joined court opinion
Joined Chief Justice Guerrero’s unanimous opinion applying the new legislation and rejecting these environmental-report objections. There was no separate writing or individual rationale. [e3]
Kelli M. Evans: Joined court opinion
Joined the same unanimous reasoning and result. The opinion records no disagreement or separate writing by her. [e3]

Reasoning: The court applied the law in force when it decided the case. It rejected an attempt to confine the social-noise rule to a particular building project while retaining the same objection to the broader plan covering residential development. The phrase “residential projects” could reasonably encompass such planning. Legislative history showed that the Legislature intended to overturn the earlier appellate decision’s treatment of residential social noise; limiting the new rule to individual buildings would undermine that purpose. The court did not need to define every possible boundary of the phrase.

The alternative-sites issue was simpler: the opponents conceded that People’s Park qualified under the new statute. The court explained that the law did not merely make that claim moot, meaning impossible to remedy. It resolved the merits against the opponents. It declined their invitation to decide how the law might apply to other future projects, which were not before the court. [e4] [e5]

Inferred practical significance: The decision removed these CEQA barriers to the People’s Park housing project and applied the residential social-noise rule to the corresponding portions of a broader university development plan. It illustrates how legislation enacted during a case can change the legal requirements an environmental report must satisfy. [e1] [e4] [e5]

Limits: The ruling did not exempt all project noise or all university development from environmental review. The report separately analyzed construction and traffic noise, which the opponents did not challenge here. The court left open whether noise from nonresidential parts of a long-range plan could be significant. It did not decide future projects’ eligibility for the alternative-site exemption. A challenge concerning lower enrollment alternatives was outside the granted review. The catalog mentions later appellate litigation; the bounded search did not verify its scope, and this summary addresses only the June 2024 Supreme Court decision. [e5] [e6]

People v. Burgos

2024-06-03 · California Supreme Court · Official opinion

Question: Does the new law requiring separate trial phases for gang enhancements apply to defendants already tried whose judgments are still on appeal? [e1]

Background: Francisco Burgos, Damon Stevenson Jr. and James Richardson were convicted of two robberies with gang enhancements, which increased their punishment. Each received 21 years in prison. Before trial, they asked to have the gang enhancements tried separately; the judge refused. While their appeals were pending, Assembly Bill 333 took effect in January 2022. It narrowed the requirements for gang liability and added Penal Code section 1109, giving defendants a right to separate phases for gang enhancements if requested. The prosecution accepted that the substantive changes applied to these pending cases and required setting aside the gang findings, but disputed whether the separate-trial rule also applied. The Court of Appeal held that it did. [e2]

Decision: By a five-to-two vote, the Supreme Court overturned the Court of Appeal’s ruling that section 1109 applies retroactively. Defendants whose trials had already occurred do not obtain the new statutory separation right merely because their judgments remain on appeal. The case returns to the Court of Appeal to decide remaining claims. This ruling did not eliminate the separate retroactive benefit of the law’s changes to the requirements for gang liability. [e3] [e2]

Justices on the Ballot

Joshua P. Groban: Joined majority opinion; Authored concurrence
Joined Guerrero’s opinion rejecting retroactive application. His concurrence, joined by Corrigan, urged lawmakers and voters adopting initiatives to specify whether new laws apply retroactively, avoiding uncertainty and repeated litigation about their intent. [e4] [e5]
Kelli M. Evans: Authored dissent
Disagreed with the result; Liu joined her dissent. She would apply section 1109 to nonfinal cases because the Legislature designed it to prevent wrongful convictions and reduce prejudice from gang evidence. She read prior retroactivity decisions as extending to laws clearly benefiting defendants on guilt or punishment, including this procedural protection. [e4] [e6]

Reasoning: California generally presumes new criminal statutes operate prospectively. Under In re Estrada, laws reducing punishment or narrowing criminal liability ordinarily benefit defendants whose judgments are not final, absent contrary intent. The majority distinguished section 1109: it changes trial sequence rather than the elements of a crime, available penalties, or an avenue for avoiding ordinary criminal punishment. Some gang evidence may remain relevant and admissible on underlying charges even in separate phases. The legislative findings about prejudice, wrongful convictions and racial disparities did not, in its view, clearly show an intent to reopen completed trials. The majority also rejected the equal-protection argument based on different treatment before and after the law’s effective date.

Evans viewed those same legislative findings as strong evidence that the law should reach existing nonfinal cases. Preventing the conviction of innocent defendants, she reasoned, benefits guilt determinations and can prevent punishment just as substantively narrowing a crime can. The majority rejected that broader application of Estrada. [e7] [e8] [e6]

Inferred practical significance: The new right to separate gang-enhancement proceedings does not itself reopen trials completed before it took effect, even when an appeal remains pending. Defendants may still pursue applicable substantive changes to gang law and other preserved challenges to prejudicial evidence. [e2] [e3] [e8]

Limits: The court expressly left Burgos’s due-process challenge to the gang evidence and other remaining claims for the Court of Appeal. It did not find the defendants innocent or decide that every use of gang evidence was proper. Groban’s request for clearer legislative drafting and Evans’s proposed retroactivity approach were separate writings. The later-history check was bounded rather than comprehensive. [e5] [e6] [e8]

Another Planet Entertainment, LLC v. Vigilant Insurance Co.

2024-05-23 · California Supreme Court · Official opinion

Question: Can the actual or potential presence of the COVID-19 virus at an insured property constitute direct physical loss or damage under a commercial property insurance policy? [e1]

Background: Another Planet operates live-entertainment venues in California and Nevada. It alleged pandemic-related closures and losses exceeding $20 million. Its insurer, Vigilant, denied coverage. The company alleged the virus physically attached to surfaces, made venues unsafe for their intended use, and triggered property and business-interruption coverage. A federal trial court dismissed its lawsuit. On appeal, the Ninth Circuit asked the California Supreme Court to resolve a California insurance-law question because state appellate decisions conflicted. The Supreme Court accepted the complaint’s factual allegations as true for this limited proceeding. [e2]

Decision: The California Supreme Court unanimously answered that the actual or potential presence of COVID-19 generally does not constitute direct physical loss or damage under a commercial property policy. Another Planet’s allegations did not establish the required injury or impairment to property. The court supplied that legal answer to the Ninth Circuit, which retained the federal appeal; it did not itself enter judgment on the federal lawsuit or award damages. It disapproved conflicting California appellate decisions to the extent they treated the alleged viral interaction or pandemic closure orders as sufficient. [e3] [e7]

Justices on the Ballot

Joshua P. Groban: Joined court opinion
Joined Chief Justice Guerrero’s opinion and its reasoning. He wrote no separate opinion. [e4]
Kelli M. Evans: Joined court opinion
Joined the same unanimous opinion. She wrote no separate opinion. [e4]

Reasoning: The policy covered physical loss or damage to property, rather than every financial loss from an interruption of business. The court read that language to require a distinct, demonstrable physical alteration that harms or impairs the property itself. Damage can be microscopic and need not affect a building’s structure. Physical loss also reaches dispossession and, in some circumstances, persistent contamination that makes property effectively unusable or uninhabitable. But inability to use property as intended does not by itself satisfy that requirement. Another Planet alleged viral bonding and danger to people without explaining physical injury to its property. Its concern about people repeatedly reintroducing the virus did not show lasting contamination inextricably connected to the premises. Closure orders changed legal permission to operate, rather than the property’s physical condition. Preventive modifications did not repair a covered loss. The broader definition of property damage in separate liability coverage, and general industry statements about pandemic exposure, did not change these property-policy terms. [e5] [e6]

Inferred practical significance: Businesses with conventional property coverage cannot establish a covered physical loss merely by alleging COVID-19 exposure, lost use, or closure orders. The decision resolves that threshold question across similar claims while leaving the particular policy language and any actual physical impairment central to coverage. [e5] [e6]

Limits: The court did not rule that COVID-19 can never physically damage any property. Its answer was bounded by these allegations and conventional policy language. It did not decide specialized communicable-disease coverage or other potentially decisive issues, including whether a covered event caused the claimed losses. Its discussion of persistent contaminants leaves room for materially different facts. Two focused official-source searches found no later modification; the resulting history check was limited. [e6] [e8]

Veverka v. Department of Veterans Affairs

2024-05-06 · First District, Division 1 · Official opinion

Question: Can an employee obtain a court declaration or attorney’s fees on a whistleblower claim when the employer proves it would have made the same decision for legitimate, independent reasons? [e1]

Background: Donald Veverka administered the state veterans home in Yountville. He reported safety and health problems, including broken elevators and inadequate heating or cooling, and what he believed were legal violations. CalVet’s undersecretary recommended his removal, citing management problems. Veverka sued, alleging unlawful retaliation. The jury found that some disclosures were legally protected and contributed to CalVet’s recommendation to remove him. But it also found, by clear and convincing evidence—a demanding proof standard—that CalVet would have made the same recommendation at that time for legitimate, independent reasons. The trial court entered judgment for CalVet. Veverka asked it to replace that judgment, arguing he still qualified for certain relief despite the same-decision finding. The court refused. [e2]

Decision: The Court of Appeal left the judgment for CalVet in place. Veverka could not obtain a declaration that CalVet violated the whistleblower statute or recover attorney’s fees and costs under it. The court dismissed CalVet’s protective cross-appeal, which offered alternative reasons to uphold the judgment, because deciding those arguments was unnecessary. It awarded CalVet its appeal costs. [e3]

Justices on the Ballot

Monique Langhorne Wilson: Authored court opinion
Wrote the unanimous opinion treating the employer’s successful same-decision showing as a complete defense under the whistleblower statutes. Humes and assigned Justice Castro joined; there was no separate writing. [e3]

Reasoning: Labor Code section 1102.6 supplies a two-step framework for whistleblower retaliation claims. First, an employee must show that protected activity contributed to the challenged action. Then the employer must prove, by clear and convincing evidence, that legitimate, independent reasons would have produced the same decision. The court read this framework as applying to the entire civil action, with no exception preserving selected remedies after the employer satisfies its burden. The first-step finding alone therefore does not establish a statutory violation. Veverka relied on a Supreme Court decision involving the Fair Employment and Housing Act, under which an employer’s same-decision defense can still leave room for declaratory relief and attorney’s fees. The court distinguished that different statute: its wording, causation standard, and remedial structure did not override the specific framework the Legislature enacted for whistleblower cases. Legislative history also supported allowing an employer to avoid liability after meeting the heightened burden. Because Veverka did not challenge the jury’s same-decision finding, that finding defeated his requested relief. Attorney’s fees were unavailable because the statute authorizes them for a successful action. [e1] [e4]

Inferred practical significance: For employees bringing this kind of whistleblower action, proving that reporting contributed to an employment decision does not by itself secure a declaration of wrongdoing or attorney’s fees. An employer that proves the statutory same-decision defense can defeat the entire claim, even though reporting played a role in its decision. [e1] [e3]

Limits: The appeal did not reconsider whether the jury correctly found legitimate, independent reasons for removal. Veverka abandoned his request for an injunction on appeal. The ruling interprets the whistleblower statutes, not the separate discrimination law discussed for comparison. This summary uses the court-designated report as corrected June 5, 2024; a standalone modification order was not supplied or located. The Supreme Court denied review August 14, with Evans favoring review; that denial does not approve the reasoning. [e2] [e4] [e5] [e6]

People v. Flores

2024-05-02 · California Supreme Court · Official opinion

Question: Did Flores’s efforts to avoid police contact in an area associated with drugs and gangs give officers reasonable suspicion to detain him? [e1]

Background: Officers saw Marlon Flores standing alone beside a parked car around 10 p.m. He looked toward them, ducked behind the car, briefly stood, and crouched again. As they approached, he remained bent over with his hands near his shoe and did not acknowledge them. Officers ordered him to stand and handcuffed him. They subsequently found suspected methamphetamine and a revolver. These facts came from the officer’s testimony and body-camera recording at a hearing on whether the evidence could be used. The trial court denied Flores’s request to exclude the evidence, treating his behavior as suspicious. Flores then pleaded no contest to carrying a loaded firearm. The Court of Appeal upheld the judgment by a divided vote. [e2]

Decision: The Supreme Court overturned the Court of Appeal’s decision upholding the judgment. Considering the circumstances together, the officers lacked a particularized, objective basis for suspecting criminal activity. The case returns to the trial court so Flores can withdraw his no-contest plea and the court can grant his motion to exclude the evidence obtained during the unlawful detention. [e3]

Justices on the Ballot

Joshua P. Groban: Joined majority opinion; Joined concurrence
Joined Corrigan’s unanimous opinion finding this detention unlawful and Evans’s separate explanation urging careful attention to why people may avoid police, including experiences of racial profiling and police violence. [e4] [e7]
Kelli M. Evans: Joined majority opinion; Authored concurrence
Agreed with the court’s ruling and wrote separately that lawful avoidance of police must be evaluated with care in its real-world context. She emphasized that people, particularly people of color, may fear injury or repeated racial profiling. Her concurrence supported the result and encouraged future arguments about how those realities inform the objective legal test. [e4] [e7]

Reasoning: The Fourth Amendment permits a brief investigative detention on reasonable suspicion, a lower threshold than proof of a crime but more than a hunch. People may decline consensual interaction with police. Unusual or evasive behavior and a neighborhood’s crime history can matter, but the whole picture must connect the person to suspected criminal activity. Here, the officer saw no exchange with another person, hiding or discarding of objects, or other conduct suggesting drug activity. There was no report of a crime in progress. Flores’s avoidance differed from the headlong flight and additional suspicious circumstances present in earlier cases. Odd behavior and location did not supply the missing connection. Officers could have continued observing or sought voluntary conversation.

Evans’s concurrence explained that avoidance may reflect fear of violence or the indignity of racial profiling. The court’s main opinion acknowledged those concerns but resolved this case under established law without deciding the broader issues. [e5] [e6] [e7]

Inferred practical significance: People retain protection against compelled police encounters when officers can identify only avoidance, unusual behavior and a neighborhood’s reputation, without enough objective grounds to suspect crime. Officers can continue observation and voluntary inquiry, and additional facts may justify a detention. [e5] [e6]

Limits: The court did not decide precisely when the detention began because it was unjustified even using the later point. It did not make evasive behavior irrelevant or establish an automatic rule against detention after flight. The concurrence’s broader discussion of racial disparities supplements, rather than replaces, the main opinion’s fact-specific holding. The bounded later-history search found no later modification but was not a complete audit. [e5] [e6] [e7]

Ruelas v. County of Alameda

2024-04-22 · California Supreme Court · Official opinion

Question: Do nonconvicted detainees working inside a county jail for a private food-service company have a California minimum-wage or overtime claim when no local ordinance sets their compensation? [e1]

Background: People detained before conviction at Alameda County’s Santa Rita Jail alleged they prepared and packaged food and cleaned an industrial kitchen for Aramark, a private company under contract with the county. The meals served jail inmates, staff and related facilities. The detainees alleged they sometimes worked more than eight hours a day or 40 hours a week but received no wages. They sued Aramark and the county in federal court. The federal trial court allowed parts of the wage claims to proceed. During an appeal before the case was finished, the Ninth Circuit asked the California Supreme Court to resolve the state-law wage question. For that purpose, the Supreme Court accepted the complaint’s factual allegations as true and assumed the work was voluntary. [e2]

Decision: The California Supreme Court unanimously answered no: these detainees had no claim for minimum wages or overtime under Labor Code section 1194 for the described work, even without a local wage ordinance. It supplied that answer to the Ninth Circuit, which retained the federal case. The opinion did not decide all the detainees’ claims or order anyone to perform unpaid labor. [e3] [e7]

Justices on the Ballot

Kelli M. Evans: Authored court opinion
Wrote the unanimous opinion interpreting the jail-compensation statute and its relationship to ordinary wage law. [e4]
Joshua P. Groban: Joined court opinion
Joined Evans’s opinion and its reasoning. He wrote no separate opinion. [e4]

Reasoning: Penal Code section 4019.3 allowed county supervisors to credit a jail inmate up to $2 for eight hours of work at the jail, while requiring no payment. The court read its broad reference to people confined or committed to jail to include detainees awaiting trial. The statute focused on who performed the work and where they performed it, rather than whether a private contractor benefited. Its words and history did not limit it to public-works programs. Ordinary minimum-wage law could not simultaneously require a wage above that statutory ceiling. The court also examined Proposition 139, which allowed public-private inmate-labor contracts. That initiative supplied wage protections for state-prison programs but did not impose the same requirements on county-jail programs. The absence of a local ordinance therefore did not make ordinary wage law apply. The justices acknowledged arguments about detainees’ financial burdens and the benefits and costs of work programs, but concluded that changing the statutory payment scheme was for lawmakers. [e5] [e6]

Inferred practical significance: For the voluntary food-service arrangement described, a private company’s role did not give nonconvicted jail workers the ordinary minimum-wage remedy. The ruling preserved the separate jail-compensation scheme rather than requiring standard wages simply because the county had adopted no wage ordinance. [e3] [e5] [e6]

Limits: The opinion assumed voluntary participation. Allegations of forced labor remained in federal court. It expressly left open work for a private company outside the county jail. The justices did not separately analyze overtime because no distinct argument was presented and premium pay depended on entitlement to regular wages. The ruling interpreted the law at the time of the 2024 decision; the limited history check was not an audit of later legislation or every remaining federal claim. The official reposted corrected version was read in full. [e7] [e8]

Temple of 1001 Buddhas v. City of Fremont

2024-03-06 · First District, Division 4 · Official opinion

Question: Did state building law require Fremont to provide a different appeal process for building-code nuisance and vacancy orders? [e1]

Background: City inspectors found unpermitted construction and other violations on a 29-acre Fremont property transferred to the Temple of 1001 Buddhas. The property included steep slopes, waterways, and areas subject to development restrictions. The city issued orders to correct nuisances and vacate certain buildings. A city-appointed hearing officer upheld 13 nuisance violations and required the owners to legalize structures where possible or remove structures that could not be legalized. Those findings were supported by evidence according to the trial court, and the owners did not properly challenge that evidentiary conclusion on appeal. Instead, they challenged the appeal process and asserted unfairness, bias, and other procedural defects. The trial court denied relief. [e2]

Decision: The Court of Appeal partly overturned the trial court’s judgment. It required court orders compelling Fremont to provide the appeal body required by state building law and to set aside the hearing decision insofar as nuisance determinations rested on building-code violations. Fremont must offer a compliant appeal for those determinations and for the vacancy order. The judgment otherwise remained in place, including the rejection of challenges affecting nuisance determinations based on zoning violations. [e3]

Justices on the Ballot

Tracie L. Brown: Authored court opinion
Wrote the unanimous opinion requiring a compliant building-code appeal process while rejecting the other grounds for overturning the administrative proceeding. [e3]
Charles A. Smiley: Joined court opinion
Joined the entire opinion and its mixed result. Served on the Court of Appeal by assignment from the Alameda County Superior Court; the opinion contains no separate explanation by him. [e3] [e6]

Reasoning: California Building Code section 1.8.8 requires appeals to a qualified appeals board or authorized agency; where none exists, the local government’s governing body must serve that function. Following an earlier decision involving Oakland, the court concluded that Fremont’s single hearing officer process did not satisfy those requirements. Calling a building-code violation a public nuisance does not remove it from state appeal protections. Adding zoning violations to the same order likewise does not eliminate the protections applicable to the building-code determinations. The missing required review was a material procedural error.

The court also concluded that a general court order enforcing the city’s mandatory duty was available alongside relief addressing this particular administrative decision. The owners’ other arguments did not establish grounds for additional relief: some were unsupported by the record, some failed to explain prejudice, and some were not properly preserved or briefed. The hearing officer’s appointment through a rotation system did not establish the alleged financial bias. [e1] [e4] [e5]

Inferred practical significance: Property owners facing building-code enforcement in Fremont must receive the type of administrative appeal required by state law, including when the city uses nuisance orders. The decision requires a lawful review process before those contested determinations can stand; it does not grant permission to maintain unpermitted structures or displace local zoning restrictions. [e1] [e3]

Limits: This was a ruling about the review process and identified procedural challenges, not a finding that the cited property conditions complied with the law. State building appeal requirements did not govern the zoning-based nuisance determinations. The court did not find that the hearing officer was biased or that the city’s attorney improperly acted as her adviser. The limited later-history search identified no official later order and was not a complete docket audit. [e3] [e5]

People v. Hardin

2024-03-04 · California Supreme Court · Official opinion

Question: Does excluding young adults sentenced to life without parole for special-circumstance murder from youth-offender parole hearings violate equal protection? Must courts first decide whether the groups being compared are similarly situated? [e1] [e3]

Background: Tony Hardin was 25 when he robbed and killed an elderly neighbor in 1989. A jury convicted him of first-degree murder and found that it occurred during a robbery, a statutory special circumstance carrying death or life without parole. He received life without parole. Decades later, he requested a proceeding to preserve evidence of his youth for a future parole hearing. California provided such hearings to many people who committed crimes before turning 26, but excluded adults sentenced to life without parole. The trial court denied his request; the Court of Appeal found the exclusion unconstitutional. [e2]

Decision: By a 5–2 vote, the Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeal. Hardin had not shown that the exclusion violated equal protection, either across all its applications or as applied to him and others convicted of special-circumstance murder. His constitutional argument therefore did not establish eligibility for a youth-offender parole hearing. The court also eliminated the separate preliminary inquiry into whether groups are similarly situated when a law expressly treats identifiable groups differently: courts should directly examine whether that difference is legally justified. [e1] [e3] [e4]

Justices on the Ballot

Joshua P. Groban: Joined majority opinion
Supported Kruger’s reasoning that the Legislature could distinguish special-circumstance murder from other crimes when deciding parole eligibility, and joined the change to the equal-protection framework. He wrote no separate opinion. [e3] [e4]
Kelli M. Evans: Authored dissent
Would have held the exclusion unconstitutional. She argued that young adults’ capacity for rehabilitation does not depend on their offense, and that the exclusion conflicted with the statute’s expressed purpose. She also argued that its disproportionate effect on Black and Brown youth, understood against the history of racially biased sentencing policies, required more searching consideration rather than unquestioning deference. Her conclusions about racial bias were part of her dissent, not findings adopted by the majority. [e5]

Reasoning: The majority applied rational-basis review, a deferential test asking whether unequal treatment has a rational connection to a legitimate governmental purpose. It read the law as balancing rehabilitation with punishment appropriate to the seriousness of the crime. Existing law treats special-circumstance murder as especially grave, so lawmakers could retain its exclusion while expanding opportunities for others. The majority accepted rough legislative distinctions and found that research questioning the breadth of special circumstances did not establish the categorical challenge presented. It rejected the separate similarly-situated threshold because that step largely duplicated the justification inquiry and created confusion. Evans disputed both the asserted punishment rationale and the adequacy of that deference. Liu wrote a separate dissent; neither ballot justice joined it. [e3] [e4] [e5] [e6]

Inferred practical significance: The ruling preserved this barrier to a parole hearing for young adults in Hardin’s position, while leaving expansion to lawmakers or different legal challenges. It also simplified the analytical steps for challenges to laws that expressly distinguish groups. Even a successful claim to parole eligibility would provide an opportunity to seek release, not automatic release. [e3] [e4] [e6]

Limits: The decision did not uphold every exclusion in the youth-offender parole law or resolve all challenges involving particular special circumstances or individual facts. It did not decide a racial-discrimination claim brought by Hardin or declare life-without-parole policy desirable. This summary describes the 2024 decision; the limited history check is not an audit of subsequent legislation or every later case. [e7]

Berlanga v. University of San Francisco

2024-02-29 · First District, Division 3 · Official opinion

Question: Did the university promise students exclusively in-person instruction during the COVID-19 emergency, and did its move to remote learning support their contract and related refund claims? [e1]

Background: University of San Francisco undergraduates attended classes on campus until March 2020, when state and local emergency orders prohibited large in-person gatherings. USF closed campus facilities and moved classes online. Students and another plaintiff brought a proposed class action seeking partial tuition refunds. They relied on admissions letters describing campus life, classroom locations in schedules and syllabi, and USF’s history of in-person teaching. The parties agreed an enrollment contract existed but disagreed about its terms. Before students paid for fall 2020 and spring 2021, USF announced that instruction would be remote or partly remote. The trial court ruled for USF on the contract and related claims without a trial. Plaintiffs voluntarily dismissed their remaining unfair-competition claim and appealed. [e2]

Decision: The Court of Appeal left the ruling for USF in place, rejecting the contract, good-faith, quasi-contract, and promissory-estoppel challenges. The plaintiffs received no tuition-refund remedy in this appeal. USF could recover its appeal costs. The unfair-competition ruling was outside the appeal. [e3]

Justices on the Ballot

Ioana Petrou: Authored court opinion
Wrote the unanimous opinion rejecting the refund claims on this record. [e4]
Victor A. Rodríguez: Joined court opinion
Joined the entire opinion and result. The report identifies no separate writing. [e4]

Reasoning: A university’s relationship with its students can create enforceable contractual obligations, but a student must identify a sufficiently specific promise. The court accepted that USF’s representations could support a promise of some campus instruction and services. They did not support an unconditional promise of exclusively in-person teaching during a global health emergency. General expectations about campus life and ordinary classroom locations did not define that obligation, and there was no evidence of a practice of teaching in person during such emergencies. For the later semesters, advance notice of remote learning also defeated a reasonable expectation of an in-person contract. The implied duty of good faith could not add a promise the contract lacked. A valid enrollment contract covering the subject prevented recovery through quasi-contract, a substitute remedy for situations without an enforceable agreement. Promissory estoppel, which can enforce a promise based on reliance, failed because no relevant promise was shown and the students had given actual payment in exchange for enrollment. [e1] [e5]

Inferred practical significance: The ruling limits these students’ ability to obtain pandemic tuition refunds from general campus descriptions and customary teaching arrangements. It leaves room for enforcement of sufficiently specific educational promises; the decisive issue here was the content of the contract shown by the evidence. [e1] [e5]

Limits: This was a decision on an evidentiary record, not merely on whether a complaint alleged a possible claim. It does not establish that every university contract permits every move online. The court did not reach USF’s other defenses or the additional plaintiff’s standing. Its unfair-competition ruling was not reviewed. The subsequent-history check was limited. [e6]

First Amendment Coalition v. Superior Court

2023-12-28 · First District, Division 3 · Official opinion

Question: May the Department of Justice withhold otherwise public police-misconduct records under statutes protecting subpoenaed documents, Inspector General materials, or unemployment-benefit information? [e1]

Background: First Amendment Coalition and KQED requested records held by the Attorney General and Department of Justice concerning specified police shootings, serious uses of force, dishonesty, and sexual assault. An earlier appeal established that the disclosure law reaches responsive records about other agencies’ officers. After further proceedings and a narrowing of the requests, the Department produced about 3,000 documents but withheld three groups: records subpoenaed from the Bakersfield Police Department during a systemic-misconduct investigation, an Inspector General report involving prison guards, and unemployment-benefit records. The trial court accepted the asserted statutory grounds for withholding. The requesters sought an appellate order requiring disclosure. [e1]

Decision: The Court of Appeal partly granted the request. It directed the trial court to set aside its judgment insofar as it permitted withholding under Government Code section 11183, the subpoena-confidentiality statute, and to conduct further proceedings. It denied the remaining requested relief. The Inspector General report could remain withheld to the extent it fell within the specified statutory exclusions, and the ruling on unemployment records remained in place. Each side had to bear its own costs. [e3]

Justices on the Ballot

Ioana Petrou: Joined court opinion
Joined the entire court opinion and its disposition; no separate writing is attributed to this justice. [e3]
Victor A. Rodríguez: Joined court opinion
Joined the entire court opinion and its disposition; no separate writing is attributed to this justice. [e3]

Reasoning: Penal Code section 832.7(b) declares designated officer records nonconfidential and available under the Public Records Act notwithstanding contrary law. That language overrides another exemption when applying it would directly conflict with the disclosure mandate. Section 11183 would effectively shield most or all misconduct records that the Department obtains using its investigative subpoena power. Applying it categorically would frustrate the transparency law. Collecting records during an investigation of systemic misconduct rather than a single incident did not itself remove them from the law.

The court distinguished exemptions that can coexist with the disclosure mandate, including the Public Records Act’s balancing provision. It also distinguished the Inspector General statute: that statute expressly places particular internal papers and records outside the universe of public records subject to the Act. The report was properly withheld insofar as those exclusions applied, although the trial court could reconsider whether portions fell outside them. For unemployment records, the requesters did not meaningfully analyze the asserted conflict or address the significance of lawyer-client confidentiality. They therefore had not shown that the trial court erred. [e1] [e2] [e3]

Inferred practical significance: People seeking covered misconduct records held by state oversight agencies gain a route to challenge blanket withholding merely because the agency obtained the records by subpoena. Access still depends on whether particular documents fall within the officer-records law and whether another valid ground supports withholding or redaction. [e1] [e2] [e3]

Limits: The court did not order immediate release of every Bakersfield document or every file from a systemic investigation. On return to the trial court, the Department could show that individual records were outside section 832.7(b) or protected for other reasons. The unemployment ruling rested on inadequate appellate argument rather than a conclusive reconciliation of the statutes. Newly added categories of misconduct records were not at issue. [e1] [e2] [e3]

Thomas v. Regents of University of California

2023-11-29 · First District, Division 2 · Official opinion

Question: Did a university soccer player adequately allege sexual harassment, negligence, breach of fiduciary duty, fraud, and negligent misrepresentation against her coach, athletic director, and university? [e1]

Background: Renee Thomas alleged that Berkeley coach Neil McGuire recruited her with assurances that she could play for four years if she met expectations. She gave up a Colorado scholarship to join Berkeley without one. She alleged repeated public berating, inappropriate comments about players’ bodies and a player’s hickey, psychological torment, and ignored complaints to administrators. After her freshman season, McGuire released her and four other players. These were allegations, not factual findings. After federal proceedings, she sued in state court. The trial court dismissed all claims after finding her pleadings legally insufficient and denied further amendment. Thomas appealed. [e1]

Decision: The court restored the sexual-harassment claim against McGuire and the Regents and returned that portion of the case for further proceedings, including amendment to identify Civil Code section 51.9 as its statutory basis. It left the dismissal of that claim against athletic director Jim Knowlton intact. It also left intact dismissal of the negligence, fiduciary-duty, fraud, and negligent-misrepresentation claims. Each side was to bear its own appellate costs. [e2]

Justices on the Ballot

Therese M. Stewart: Authored majority opinion
Wrote the controlling opinion, joined by Justice Richman. It held the existing factual allegations sufficient to support a sexual-harassment claim, subject to clarification of the statutory basis. Judge Markman separately agreed that amendment should be allowed but disagreed that the existing allegations adequately connected the bullying to gender; he would require additional facts, not merely a corrected statutory label. [e3]

Reasoning: California pleading rules require courts to accept properly alleged facts and reasonable inferences without deciding whether a plaintiff can prove them. Section 51.9 reaches severe or pervasive gender-based hostile conduct in specified professional or service relationships; it does not require sexual advances or explicitly sexual remarks. Considered together, the allegations of pervasive bullying, comments implicating gender stereotypes, and gender as a substantial motivating factor adequately notified McGuire of the claim. Intent was especially within his knowledge. Allegations that university administrators ignored complaints also supported employer liability through ratification. They did not establish that McGuire was Knowlton’s agent personally.

The remaining theories had different defects. Thomas did not develop the policy analysis necessary to extend the university’s protective duty to the nonphysical harm alleged, and her negligence argument concerning McGuire was abandoned or inadequately presented. Trust in a coach and the ordinary coach-player relationship did not establish an undertaking to put her interests ahead of teammates’ competing interests. Misrepresentation immunity covered the scholarship, educational-cost, and career-related financial interests alleged. Speculation about an admissions scandal did not connect corruption by McGuire to her alleged loss. She did not show how amendments would cure the remaining defects. [e4]

Inferred practical significance: A student athlete with adequately alleged gender-based hostile treatment can pursue a section 51.9 claim beyond the initial pleading stage even when much of the alleged abuse is not explicitly sexual. Institutional inaction may support a ratification theory, but personal liability of an administrator and other legal theories still require their own factual and legal foundations. [e2] [e4]

Limits: The ruling did not find that harassment occurred or that gender motivated the coach; Thomas still had to prove her claim. It did not decide whether Berkeley is a business establishment under the Unruh Act. The negligence discussion expressly left open whether a university could owe a duty concerning nonphysical injuries on adequately developed arguments. Review denial does not endorse the court’s reasoning. [e4] [e5]

People v. Peterson

2023-09-26 · First District, Division 3 · Official opinion

Question: Could the defendant’s remarks, Facebook post, and mailed political criticism support a stalking conviction consistent with the First Amendment? [e1]

Background: Bruce Peterson attended an open house supporting a school bond measure at the home of a Lafayette city councilmember and his wife. He made an unsettling comment about how long it had been since the wife’s birthday. He later reposted a publicly available family photograph, referred to the couple’s daughters, and mailed a rambling letter criticizing local politicians with a check payable to anyone who was not corrupt. The wife and councilmember testified that the communications frightened them, particularly the references to their children. The birthday and family information were publicly available on Facebook. Defense witnesses described Peterson as unusual, distrustful of government, and given to exaggerated language, but nonviolent. A jury convicted him of stalking. The trial court imposed two years of probation, including one year of home confinement. [e2]

Decision: The Court of Appeal overturned the judgment because the evidence was insufficient to support stalking: Peterson’s speech and related acts were constitutionally protected on these facts. The disposition reversed the judgment without ordering a new trial. The court did not decide his remaining challenges. [e3]

Justices on the Ballot

Victor A. Rodríguez: Authored court opinion
Wrote the unanimous opinion applying First Amendment protections to the charged communications and reversing the conviction. Tucher and Fujisaki joined; there was no separate writing. [e4]

Reasoning: The charged form of stalking required harassment, a credible threat, and an intent to put the target in reasonable fear for personal or immediate-family safety. The statute excludes constitutionally protected activity. A true threat of violence lacks First Amendment protection, but the court independently examined whether a reasonable listener would understand these communications, in their full context, as a serious expression of intent to commit unlawful violence. This constitutional review still respected the jury’s credibility determinations. The prosecution’s case rested entirely on speech and its dissemination in the context of a school bond measure, local politics, and criticism of a politician. The birthday remark was odd, but did not convey violence. The family photograph and questions about the children were disturbing, but their political context and content did not suggest even an implied threat to their safety. The letter and check criticized corruption; the prosecution’s proposed threatening subtext lacked evidentiary support. The communications also did not become a true threat when considered together. The family’s actual fear therefore did not itself establish the constitutionally required threat. [e1] [e5]

Inferred practical significance: The decision protects political expression from a stalking conviction when the communications, viewed in context, do not communicate a true threat of violence. It requires an appellate court to examine that constitutional boundary independently where the prosecution rests on expressive acts, even when the recipients understandably find those acts alarming. [e1] [e5]

Limits: The ruling turns on these particular communications and surrounding circumstances. It does not require an explicit threat: a threat may be implied in an appropriate context. The prosecution did not pursue stalking based on repeated following. The Attorney General separately conceded error in the trial court’s answer to a jury question, but the court found it unnecessary to decide the other appellate claims after finding insufficient evidence. [e6]

People v. Pomar

2023-09-13 · First District, Division 5 · Official opinion

Question: Did the trial courts act within their discretion by disqualifying the entire San Francisco District Attorney’s Office from two prosecutions because of the district attorney’s conflict of interest? [e1]

Background: Jerome Mallory, the cousin of Brooke Jenkins’s husband, died in a drive-by shooting. The District Attorney’s Office charged Sincere Pomar and Stevie Mitchell with his murder and related offenses. Jenkins, then an assistant district attorney, was kept apart from that prosecution. After resigning to campaign for the recall of District Attorney Chesa Boudin, she publicly criticized the office’s handling of the case, including its decision to drop a gang charge. She also linked Pomar’s release to additional crimes alleged in a separate prosecution. Jenkins later became district attorney. Trial courts disqualified her entire office from both prosecutions, despite an information barrier in the Mallory case. The Attorney General appealed those orders. [e1]

Decision: The Court of Appeal left both disqualification orders in place. The San Francisco office remained barred from prosecuting the Mallory case and the separate Pomar prosecution. The decision resolved who could prosecute, rather than whether the defendants committed the charged offenses. [e3]

Justices on the Ballot

Danny Y. Chou: Authored court opinion
Wrote the court opinion explaining the disposition and its legal grounds. [e3]
Gordon Burns: Joined court opinion
Joined the entire court opinion and its disposition; no separate writing is attributed to this justice. [e3]

Reasoning: Penal Code section 1424 requires a conflict serious enough to make fair treatment unlikely. Removing an entire office requires an especially persuasive showing; an appearance of impropriety is insufficient. But the inquiry covers discretionary decisions such as plea offers and sentencing recommendations as well as trial conduct.

The district attorney’s family connection alone did not require removal of her office. The combination of that personal interest, her widely publicized criticism of the charging decisions, and her authority over deputies’ hiring, firing, and promotion supported the trial courts’ findings. Deputies could consciously or unconsciously feel pressure to prosecute more aggressively in accordance with their supervisor’s publicly expressed views. An information barrier could not erase statements already known publicly. No proof that she had actually directed a deputy to act unfairly was required, because the statute seeks to prevent unfairness before it occurs.

The second prosecution presented a closer question because Jenkins was unrelated to its victims. Her public statements nevertheless connected that prosecution to the death of her husband’s cousin and to her criticism of Pomar’s treatment. The appellate court deferred to the trial judges’ supported assessment of the local circumstances and likely effect on deputies. [e2]

Inferred practical significance: A defendant can obtain removal of a whole prosecutor’s office when supported findings show that the elected district attorney’s personal interest and public statements create a likelihood of unfair treatment that an information barrier cannot adequately address. The decision also illustrates the substantial latitude trial judges have in assessing those circumstances. [e2] [e3]

Limits: The ruling did not find ethical misconduct by Jenkins or the deputies; the trial court expressly found no such violation. It did not establish that every public comment or family connection disqualifies an office. The court acknowledged that these trial judges could reasonably have reached a different discretionary result. A September 29 modification corrected which party sought calendar preference, without changing the judgment. [e1] [e2]

Pico Neighborhood Association v. City of Santa Monica

2023-08-24 · California Supreme Court · Official opinion

Question: Must a protected class constitute a majority or near majority of a hypothetical district to prove vote dilution under the California Voting Rights Act, and what alternative electoral system must plaintiffs identify? [e2]

Background: Santa Monica elected its seven council members at large in staggered elections. Latino residents represented approximately 14 percent of the city's citizen voting-age population and 30 percent of the proposed Pico district. Pico Neighborhood Association and resident Maria Loya challenged the system under the California Voting Rights Act (CVRA) and equal protection principles. After a six-week trial, the trial court found racially polarized voting and unlawful dilution, and ordered a special election using seven districts. The Court of Appeal stayed and reversed that judgment, reasoning that Latino voters could not constitute a majority in any proposed district. It did not decide whether the elections were racially polarized. [e1]

Decision: The Supreme Court unanimously reversed the Court of Appeal and remanded for reconsideration under the correct legal standard. A CVRA plaintiff need not establish a majority or near majority in a hypothetical district. The plaintiff must identify a lawful alternative electoral system under which the protected class would have the potential to elect its preferred candidate, either alone or with crossover support. The court did not determine that Santa Monica violated the CVRA or reinstate a particular remedial map. [e2] [e3]

Justices on the Ballot

Kelli M. Evans: Authored court opinion
Authored the unanimous court opinion. [e3]
Joshua P. Groban: Joined court opinion
Joined the court opinion without a separate writing. [e3]

Reasoning: The CVRA deliberately provides broader protection than the federal Voting Rights Act. Its text rejects geographical compactness as a prerequisite and protects both the ability to elect and the ability to influence an election. Importing a majority-minority district requirement would defeat that legislative choice. Nonpartisan elections may be won with a plurality, and minority voters may elect their preferred candidate with support from other voters.

Racially polarized voting and dilution remain distinct requirements. Plaintiffs must offer a reasonable, lawful alternative as a benchmark against which the existing system can be assessed. Alternatives may include district elections, cumulative voting, limited voting, or ranked choice voting. A searching appraisal of local circumstances must examine electoral history, political cohesion, crossover voting, likely candidates, winning thresholds, and the alternative system's actual potential. An increase in a group's population percentage alone does not show dilution when it still provides no realistic electoral opportunity. The comparison must account for the protected class's overall electoral opportunities, including losses elsewhere that offset an apparent gain. Establishing a benchmark at the liability stage does not conclusively select the final remedy. [e2]

Inferred practical significance: The decision permits CVRA claims by minority groups that cannot form majority districts, while requiring a concrete electoral alternative and a fact-specific showing of improved opportunity. It makes actual electoral potential central to the dilution inquiry. [e2]

Limits: The court expressed no view on whether Santa Monica's system ultimately violated the CVRA. The Court of Appeal must address dilution, racially polarized voting, and unresolved appellate issues. The court declined to define the independent ability-to-influence theory because plaintiffs had not presented such a theory distinct from their ability-to-elect claim. The September 20 modification revised only the explanation of ranked choice voting in footnote 8 and did not affect the judgment. [e3] [e4]

SHR St. Francis, LLC v. City and County of San Francisco

2023-08-17 · First District, Division 5 · Official opinion

Question: Did San Francisco’s hotel property-tax valuation improperly include nontaxable business assets associated with management, cancellation charges, in-room movies, and guest laundry? [e1]

Background: A 2015 ownership change triggered reassessment of the Westin St. Francis hotel. The assessor valued it at about $795 million using expected operating income converted into present value. The hotel’s owners challenged the assessment, arguing that it included the value of four business assets that should not be subject to property tax. The assessment appeals board largely rejected that position. It deducted management fees and treated cancellation charges, movies, and laundry income as part of the hotel’s taxable value. An adjustment to the rate used to convert income to value reduced the assessment to about $785 million. The owners sought a tax refund and a new assessment in court. The trial court upheld the board’s determination, and the owners appealed. [e2]

Decision: The Court of Appeal partly overturned the judgment. The valuation improperly included at least some value from the management agreement, in-room movies, and guest laundry services. It upheld inclusion of cancellation, no-show, and early-departure income. The matter returned for a reassessment hearing; the board could reopen the record for additional valuation evidence. The owners were awarded appeal costs. The court did not set a replacement valuation or a specific refund. [e3]

Justices on the Ballot

Danny Y. Chou: Authored court opinion
Wrote the unanimous opinion requiring reassessment of the three business assets while permitting inclusion of cancellation-related income. [e4]
Gordon Burns: Joined court opinion
Joined the entire opinion and its mixed result, including the reassessment requirement. The report contains no separate explanation. [e4]

Reasoning: California law permits an assessor to assume the presence of rights needed to use property productively, but forbids directly taxing the value of exempt intangible business assets. Because the owners attacked a valuation method inherently unable to remove that value, the court reviewed the legal method independently. Deducting management fees alone did not show that the management agreement’s entire value had been removed. An investment ordinarily produces a return above its costs. The city supplied no evidence that the fees captured that additional value, and the board’s general rate adjustment did not cure the problem. The contracts for movies and laundry likewise produced identifiable business income, separate from the real estate itself, and at least part of their value had to be excluded. Cancellation-related charges were different. They paid for a right to possess and use a room during an agreed period, even if the guest did not exercise that right. They therefore related directly to the taxable real property and could remain in its valuation. [e1] [e5]

Inferred practical significance: For hotel assessments using projected income, the decision requires a supported separation of exempt business value from taxable real estate. Simply subtracting associated expenses may leave taxable value overstated. At the same time, income tied directly to the right to occupy a room remains part of the property valuation. [e1] [e5]

Limits: The court did not approve the owners’ proposed additional deduction of 20 percent of management fees or determine what portions of movie and laundry income must be excluded. Those valuation questions remained for the board. The official report says the opinion incorporates the September 13, 2023 modification; rehearing was denied that day and Supreme Court review was denied November 15, 2023. Denial of review does not itself endorse the reasoning. [e6]

Lacy v. City and County of San Francisco

2023-08-08 · First District, Division 5 · Official opinion

Question: May San Francisco authorize resident noncitizen parents and guardians to vote in local school-board elections under its city charter? [e1]

Background: San Francisco voters approved Proposition N in 2016. It allowed qualifying adult noncitizen residents who are parents, guardians, or caregivers of children under 19 living in the school district to vote in school-board elections. The charter amendment initially had a sunset date but permitted continuation by ordinance, which the Board of Supervisors adopted. Noncitizens voted in several school-board elections. In 2022, challengers sued, arguing the measure violated the California Constitution and state election statutes. The trial court agreed and declared the implementing ordinance unenforceable. San Francisco appealed. [e1]

Decision: The Court of Appeal overturned that judgment and directed the trial court to enter a new judgment for San Francisco. The city recovered its appeal costs. Proposition N survived the constitutional and statutory challenges addressed in the opinion. An August 28 modification added an explanation of why further briefing on vote dilution was unnecessary and denied rehearing, without changing the judgment. [e3]

Justices on the Ballot

Mark Simons: Authored court opinion
Wrote the court opinion explaining the disposition and its legal grounds. [e3]
Gordon Burns: Joined court opinion
Joined the entire court opinion and its disposition; no separate writing is attributed to this justice. [e3]
Danny Y. Chou: Joined court opinion
Joined the entire court opinion and its disposition; no separate writing is attributed to this justice. [e3]

Reasoning: The state Constitution says a United States citizen who is 18 and resides in California may vote. The court read that as protecting those voters without expressly or necessarily prohibiting expansion of the electorate to noncitizens. Unlike Congress, the California Legislature has broad lawmaking power unless the state Constitution restricts it. The text and constitutional history did not establish the claimed prohibition. The court distinguished an older decision concerning specific residency and naturalization waiting periods and declined to follow broader language in that decision that was unnecessary to its result.

A separate question was whether a charter city possessed authority to expand this electorate. Constitutional provisions permit charter cities to determine the manner of selecting school-board members. Reading their text and history together with home-rule provisions, the court concluded that authority included this expansion of voter qualifications. Education statutes also recognize controlling charter provisions, so the general statutory citizenship requirements did not invalidate Proposition N.

The court rejected equal-protection arguments that adding noncitizen voters unlawfully diluted citizens’ votes. It applied the test asking whether the measure had a rational connection to a legitimate purpose. Voters could reasonably believe that involving parents in school elections would improve participation and educational outcomes. A separate suggestion of racial vote dilution was speculative. The modification explained that the parties had an opportunity to address the issue in responding to supporting briefs, satisfying the requirement for an opportunity to be heard. [e2]

Inferred practical significance: The ruling permits San Francisco to include these qualifying noncitizen residents in school-board elections. Its constitutional analysis gives charter cities room to respond to local educational interests through their charter election provisions, subject to other constitutional protections. [e2] [e3]

Limits: The holding concerns the specified local school-board electorate. It does not authorize noncitizen voting in federal elections or decide every possible expansion of local voting. The court did not decide whether charter cities could narrow the franchise or whether discriminatory intent would alter the result; no party claimed such intent here. It assessed legal validity rather than whether the policy was wise. [e1] [e2]

People v. Vaesau

2023-08-04 · First District, Division 1 · Official opinion

Question: May a trial court allow a district attorney to withdraw a resentencing recommendation before deciding its merits, and what justification must support withdrawal? [e1] [e3]

Background: John Vaesau was convicted in 1992 of attempted murders and other offenses committed when he was 16. He received two life terms with parole eligibility plus 14 years. In April 2022, San Francisco District Attorney Chesa Boudin recommended recall and resentencing under what became Penal Code section 1172.1. After voters recalled Boudin, successor Brooke Jenkins asked to withdraw the recommendation. The office offered no substantive explanation beyond a new prosecutor’s comment that the papers were thin. A prior prosecutor had described Vaesau’s youth, remorse, personal development and other mitigating circumstances at a parole hearing. The trial court allowed withdrawal without deciding whether his sentence should change. [e1]

Decision: The Court of Appeal set aside the order permitting withdrawal and returned the case for reconsideration. It required the trial court to evaluate whether the district attorney had a legitimate basis to withdraw and to exercise its own discretion. It did not order resentencing or require a particular result on the renewed withdrawal request. The withdrawal order was appealable because terminating the proceeding affected Vaesau’s substantial rights. [e2]

Justices on the Ballot

Kathleen M. Banke: Joined court opinion
Joined Presiding Justice Humes’s opinion and its disposition with assigned Judge Bowen. The report attributes no separate writing or individual rationale to Banke. [e4]

Reasoning: A qualifying recommendation restores the court’s authority to reconsider a final sentence. The district attorney therefore cannot automatically end the proceeding merely by withdrawing support: sentencing authority belongs to the court, and unilateral executive control would raise separation-of-powers concerns. Nor is a resentencing recommendation equivalent to a civil plaintiff’s lawsuit that the plaintiff may simply dismiss.

The opposite categorical rule also failed. Section 1172.1’s presumption favoring recall and resentencing governs the merits; it does not force courts to decide the merits of every recommendation despite procedural problems, such as a recommendation submitted for the wrong person. Courts retain authority to dismiss without prejudice in appropriate circumstances. Vaesau had received notice and a hearing addressing withdrawal, so the statute’s hearing requirements did not themselves mandate a merits hearing.

Withdrawal nevertheless requires a legitimate explanation assessed case by case. Administrative error, changed law or changed prisoner circumstances might qualify. A simple change of position does not. The statute recognizes the scrutiny behind referrals, and due process protects against arbitrary government action. Here, the record did not show substantive reevaluation and the court may not have understood its full discretion to refuse withdrawal. Reconsideration was therefore necessary. [e3]

Inferred practical significance: A change in district attorney does not automatically erase an existing resentencing recommendation. Defendants retain the benefit of judicial consideration of the reasons for withdrawal, while prosecutors may seek withdrawal on a legitimate basis and courts may permit it before ruling on the merits. [e3]

Limits: The decision concerns withdrawal before a merits ruling under the statutory version discussed. It does not decide whether Vaesau deserves a shorter sentence or whether the new district attorney could establish a valid reason on remand. The court did not need to resolve his separate prosecutorial-ethics argument. [e3]

Traiman v. Alameda Unified School District

2023-08-03 · First District, Division 5 · Official opinion

Question: Does a uniform school parcel-tax formula based on building size become unlawful because it caps the total tax payable for each parcel? [e1]

Background: Alameda Unified School District voters approved Measure A in March 2020 to support increased teacher and staff salaries. The seven-year tax charged improved parcels 26.5 cents per building square foot, capped at $7,999 per parcel, and vacant parcels $299. Leland Traiman sued to invalidate the measure. He argued that the cap effectively created two classes: smaller buildings paying the full square-foot rate and larger buildings paying a lower effective rate once the cap was reached. The trial court accepted that argument. It invalidated the measure except for the vacant-property tax and awarded Traiman $374,960 in attorney fees as a successful public-interest plaintiff. The district appealed both rulings. Earlier Alameda school tax measures and court decisions formed part of the dispute, but the appeal concerned the distinct 2020 measure. [e2]

Decision: The Court of Appeal overturned the judgment invalidating the tax and also reversed the attorney-fee award. Measure A’s capped square-foot formula satisfied the statutory requirement of uniform application. The court did not need to decide the district’s alternative arguments about prior judgments, severing invalid provisions, or independent objections to the fee award. [e3]

Justices on the Ballot

Danny Y. Chou: Authored court opinion
Wrote the unanimous opinion upholding the capped tax formula and reversing the fee award. [e4]
Gordon Burns: Joined court opinion
Joined the entire opinion and result. No separate writing appears in the report. [e4]

Reasoning: Government Code section 50079 permits school districts, with two-thirds voter approval, to impose qualified special taxes applying uniformly to taxpayers or property, subject to specified exceptions. The court read that requirement to demand the same tax formula for everyone covered, rather than identical effective rates or outcomes. Every nonexempt improved parcel was subject to the same rate and cap. The measure did not assign different formulas to residential and commercial property or other express classes. An earlier case, Borikas, had invalidated an Alameda measure that explicitly created property classes and taxed them differently. It had not held a cap inherently unlawful. Other case law accepted square-foot taxation even though arithmetic produced different tax bills. Legislative history supported school taxing authority while restricting discriminatory classifications; it did not indicate an intent to forbid caps. The court also reasoned that treating every difference in effective rate as a prohibited classification would undermine familiar flat and square-foot taxes. The cap limited everyone’s potential liability under the same formula. [e5]

Inferred practical significance: The decision permits this school district to use one capped square-foot formula across improved properties. A lower effective rate for a large building after it reaches the cap does not, by itself, defeat statutory uniformity. The ruling preserves the distinction between differing results under one formula and express property classifications taxed under different formulas. [e5]

Limits: The holding concerns the formula and cap in the 2020 measure under section 50079. A separate challenge to exemptions had already been dismissed and was not part of this appeal. The court did not decide whether judgments validating earlier measures independently barred this lawsuit. The official report records Supreme Court review denied October 25, 2023; denial does not itself endorse the reasoning. [e6]

Boermeester v. Carry

2023-07-31 · California Supreme Court · Official opinion

Question: Did common-law fair procedure require a private university to offer a live hearing with direct or indirect cross-examination in the accused student’s presence before expelling him? [e1]

Background: The University of Southern California expelled Matthew Boermeester after investigating an allegation of intimate-partner violence. The administrative record included the alleged victim’s initial account, her later recantation, witness accounts, surveillance video, and Boermeester’s explanation that the encounter was playful. USC offered him access to evidence with an attorney-adviser, an individual hearing, and an opportunity to submit questions for the alleged victim’s separate hearing. He declined the individual hearing and questioning opportunity in favor of a written response. The trial court rejected his challenge, but a divided Court of Appeal ruled that USC had to provide real-time questioning at a live hearing. The Supreme Court reviewed that procedural requirement. [e1]

Decision: The Supreme Court unanimously overturned the Court of Appeal’s judgment. It held that common-law fair procedure did not require the particular live hearing and cross-examination procedure imposed by that court. It returned the case to the Court of Appeal to decide Boermeester’s remaining appellate claims, which that court had not reached. The Supreme Court therefore did not finally dispose of every challenge to his expulsion. [e3]

Justices on the Ballot

Joshua P. Groban: Authored court opinion
Wrote the court opinion explaining the disposition and its legal grounds. [e3]
Kelli M. Evans: Joined court opinion
Joined the entire court opinion and its disposition; no separate writing is attributed to this justice. [e3]

Reasoning: Private universities provide an important educational service and can substantially affect students’ educational and professional opportunities. They must follow common-law fair procedure when imposing discipline: adequate notice and a meaningful opportunity to respond. But this flexible doctrine does not require all the procedures of a court trial. Constitutional due process did not directly apply to USC because the case involved no state action.

Universities retain primary responsibility for choosing a fair process that balances an accused student’s interests, the complainant’s interests, witness participation, campus safety, and institutional resources. Mandatory real-time adversarial questioning could discourage participation or cause renewed trauma, and private universities lack courts’ subpoena power and trial resources. USC offered multiple means to review and respond to evidence. It was not required to add a hearing where Boermeester contemporaneously observed and questioned witnesses, either physically or virtually. The court disapproved inconsistent language in an earlier appellate decision.

The court left open whether indirect questioning outside a live hearing might sometimes be necessary. Assuming such a duty concerning third-party witnesses, any omission here was harmless: the alleged victim’s initial statement, consistent video, and Boermeester’s admissions supported the university’s finding of physical harm. He had an opportunity to submit questions for the alleged victim herself, and USC could credit her initial account over her recantation. [e2]

Inferred practical significance: Private universities retain flexibility to design disciplinary procedures that provide meaningful notice and response without necessarily staging courtroom-style live cross-examination. Students can still challenge whether the procedures actually provided were fair and whether the institution followed its rules. [e2] [e3]

Limits: The holding addressed this common-law requirement for a private university. It did not decide all claims of unfairness, whether every case could omit an individual hearing, or every circumstance requiring indirect written questions. Later state legislation and federal regulations discussed in the opinion did not govern these events; this summary does not describe current Title IX requirements. The United States Supreme Court’s later refusal to hear the case did not approve the reasoning. [e1] [e2]
